title: Sunk Cost Fallacy
hook: Already spent is a receipt, not a reason to keep drilling into bad ground.
counterintuition: Past cost feels like evidence because pain wants a purpose. Clear judgment moves the receipt out of the decision and asks what the next dollar can still buy.
tryThisNow: Take one draining commitment and write two columns: unrecoverable cost, and next cost. Decide only from the second column.
keyTakeaway: Ignore costs you cannot recover; the only live decision is whether the next hour, dollar, or risk is still worth paying.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ben stands beside a forecast grid on the drilling platform while the safety lead points to another week of unstable pressure readings. The well has already eaten four months and a frightening amount of money. That sentence is true. It is also irrelevant to the next safety choice.

The sunk cost fallacy begins when past spending starts arguing for future spending. The money, time, pride, and effort are gone. They can teach you, but they cannot vote.

The next cost is the only cost still alive.

Ask what you would choose if you arrived today with no need to justify yesterday. If the answer changes, the receipt has been steering.
breakdown.deepRead:
The forecast grid has two colors: red for pressure risk, blue for money already spent. Ben notices that the room keeps looking at the blue. The operations chief says they are too deep to stop now. The safety lead says stopping for a week may prevent a blowout. Both statements feel heavy, but only one points forward.

Sunk cost is the cost you cannot get back. It may be money in a half-built tool, years in a weak career path, tickets for a trip you no longer want, or reputation attached to a public plan. The trap is emotional accounting. Stopping makes the old cost feel wasted, so continuing feels like rescuing it.

You cannot rescue yesterday's money by endangering tomorrow's money.

The useful question is brutally narrow: from this point forward, would I pay the next cost for the expected next benefit? If yes, continue. If no, stop, shrink, sell, pause, or redesign. The prior cost may explain why the choice feels painful. It does not improve the future payoff.

An orchestra panel can feel the same pull. Camille has a donor pledge card beside the audition list. The donor has funded a search for a star violinist, and the committee has spent six months flying candidates in. The best applicant today is steady but wrong for the program. Camille writes non-refundable on the pledge card and asks the panel to score only the next season's fit. The airfare is gone. The wrong hire would keep charging interest.

Persistence is a virtue only when the future case still works.
breakdown.fullRead:
The water district bid review has a shift roster taped to the wall because three crews have already spent nights preparing for a vendor's pilot. Thomas, the project engineer, can feel the room leaning toward approval. Nobody wants to admit that the bid now looks worse than it did in January. The software integration is late, the maintenance contract is vague, and the backup pumps still require manual logging.

Thomas writes Concorde fallacy beside the crew roster.

That name fits any project that becomes harder to stop because it has already consumed so much. The past spending turns into a courtroom speech: after all this work, after all this money, after all these promises, how can we quit? But the past is not a hostage you can save by paying more. It is a record of what happened.

H. R. Arkes and C. Blumer's classic work, The Psychology of Sunk Cost, made the trap plain with non-refundable ski trips. When people imagined paying more for one trip and less for another on the same date, many felt pulled toward the more expensive trip even when it was less appealing. The money already spent changed the emotional weight of the choice, even though the money could not be recovered.

You have felt this without skis. You keep watching the bad film because you paid for the ticket. You finish the heavy meal because it was expensive. You keep a contractor because switching would make the first deposit feel foolish. You stay in a strategy meeting because the plan has already taken three quarters and your name is on the first slide.

Here is the clean test: if the past cost had been paid by someone else, what would you do next?

That question strips pride from the decision. It does not erase responsibility. You can still learn why the cost was paid, apologize for the mistake, report it clearly, or change the process that allowed it. But none of those duties require throwing good resources after bad ones.

A game studio retention board sees this when Isabel reviews a failing feature. The team has spent nine months building a guild system players barely use. The risk register is full of old promises: launch trailer, investor demo, creator partnerships. Isabel marks future cost and asks what another three months would buy. The answer is not enough. The feature gets cut, and the saved team moves to onboarding bugs that new players actually hit.

The hard part is social. Ending the project exposes the old decision. Continuing hides it for a little longer. That is why sunk cost survives in smart rooms: the next payment purchases delay from embarrassment.

Clear judgment refuses that bargain.

Use the past as tuition, not as a steering wheel. Keep the lesson, close the leak, and make the next choice from the ground under your feet. The cost that matters is the one still waiting to be paid.

examples.scenario: The forecast grid on the rig wall shows pressure risk in red and four months of sunk spend in blue. Ben, the drilling supervisor, hears the operations chief say they are too deep to pause. He writes sunk cost across the blue column. The safety lead is waiting, and Ben has to choose between another shift underground or a stop-work order based only on future risk.
examples.whatToDo: Move the blue column out of the decision. Judge the next shift by pressure risk, crew safety, and expected benefit, not by money already gone.
examples.whyItMatters: The prior spend cannot make the well safer or more valuable. It only makes stopping feel humiliating, which is exactly why it must be separated.

reviewCards.front: What is the one question that cuts through sunk cost?
reviewCards.back: From this point forward, would the next cost be worth the next benefit? If the answer is no, the money, time, or pride already spent cannot make continuing rational.

reviewCards.front: You paid for a ticket and no longer want to go. What part of the decision is still alive?
reviewCards.back: The travel, time, safety, and enjoyment still ahead. The ticket price is already gone, so it should not force you into spending the evening badly too.

reviewCards.front: Why does stopping a bad project feel so hard even when the future case is weak?
reviewCards.back: Stopping makes the past loss visible. Continuing often buys delay from embarrassment, which feels like protecting the investment even though it adds new cost.

reviewCards.front: A team has spent months on a feature users ignore. What comparison should guide the next sprint?
reviewCards.back: Compare the expected value of one more sprint on that feature with the expected value of the best alternative use of the team. Past months belong in the lesson file, not the sprint decision.

reviewCards.front: How can you respect past effort without obeying it?
reviewCards.back: Record what the effort taught, thank the people involved, and fix the process that led to the loss. Then decide the next move using only future cost and future benefit.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to move unrecoverable costs out of the live decision. The skill is separating accountability for the past from allocation of the next hour, dollar, person, or risk.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a project defense starts with what has already been spent, then ask what the next unit of time or money will buy from today.
If you feel pulled to use a non-refundable purchase, then compare the remaining experience with staying home, reselling, or choosing the better alternative.
If you stay in a draining commitment because of years already invested, then write the next six months of costs and benefits as if you were advising a friend.
If a course or degree feels wrong, then compare the next term with the best alternative path from today, not with tuition already paid.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Choose one commitment you are defending with already. Write what is unrecoverable, then write the next cost. Make one small decision using only the next cost.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one project, purchase, or commitment. Label sunk costs in one color and future costs in another, then make the next decision from the future color.

memorableLines.text: The next cost is the only cost still alive.
memorableLines.why: It gives the reader a short rule for separating unrecoverable past spending from the live choice.

memorableLines.text: You cannot rescue yesterday's money by endangering tomorrow's money.
memorableLines.why: The line makes the emotional mistake vivid without using technical language.

memorableLines.text: Use the past as tuition, not as a steering wheel.
memorableLines.why: It preserves learning from failure while refusing to let old cost control the next move.
